title: Council Post: From Shortcuts To Strategic Edge: Redefining The AI Journey For Competitive Advantage
text:
CEO of Qlik, driving the mission to create a data-literate world where organizations tackle their most complex challenges with data.
In a landscape where artificial intelligence (AI) ignites imaginations and promises to redefine industries, several news sources have heralded a note of caution, such as this article published by Seeking Alpha, examining the early adopters of certain AI tools. Their experiences highlight the crucial misconception that AI can be a mere add-on—a plug-and-play solution for instant business transformation.
The article underscores the gap between expectation and reality. The essential dialogue shouldn't center on AI's potential efficacy alone but rather on the depth of our investment in its foundational requirements.
True transformation through AI isn't borne from superficial implementations—it necessitates a commitment to data integrity, governance and strategic foresight. A short-term approach to AI integration not only diminishes its potential but also jeopardizes our competitive edge on the global stage.
In this article, I delve into the foundational shifts vital for harnessing AI's true potential. Business leaders can expect advice aimed at directing their teams toward leveraging AI technologies effectively, ensuring that their journey into AI transcends mere fascination to achieve real, sustainable value.
Shortcuts In AI: A Misguided Approach To Innovation
The journey toward leveraging AI's full potential is fraught with misconceptions, particularly the allure of shortcuts promising swift, transformative results. Companies, driven by a desire for quick gains, often gravitate toward off-the-shelf AI solutions such as generic analytics tools, plug-and-play chatbots or pre-built machine learning models. These are perceived as easy wins, offering a competitive advantage with minimal initial effort. However, this approach is significantly flawed.
Unlike the deliberate, phased implementation that tests AI's waters through controlled, area-specific applications, shortcuts bypass the essential groundwork for successful AI integration. Phased implementation is prudent, allowing organizations to learn, adapt and scale AI solutions responsibly. In contrast, adopting superficial solutions without adequate customization or backend integration can lead to disillusionment, wasted resources and strategic missteps.
For AI to deliver on its promise, a shift in focus is essential—from the appeal of quick fixes to the substantial, albeit more challenging, task of building a robust AI ecosystem from the ground up. By moving beyond the superficial application of AI technologies, companies can unlock genuine innovation and sustainable competitive advantage, ensuring that their investment in AI isn't just a fleeting experiment but a cornerstone of their future growth and success.
Building A Strong Foundation: The Key To AI Success
Establishing a strong foundation for AI requires focusing on comprehensive data management and fostering a cultural shift toward embracing AI and ensuring its strategic integration within the organization. This approach helps ensure not just the technological readiness for AI but also aligns it with the broader goals and values of the company, making AI a fundamental part of its growth and innovation strategy.
Data Management
At the core of AI's success is a strong data management foundation. Take, for instance, our approach when we worked with a major healthcare provider to use machine learning and predictive analytics to identify patients at risk of missing appointments. By analyzing vast, varied datasets, they could proactively engage with these individuals, significantly reducing no-shows and enhancing patient care. This example underscores the importance of not just collecting but intelligently curating and analyzing data to inform AI-driven outcomes.
Cultural Shift
Equally important is fostering a culture that embraces data-driven decision-making and strategic alignment throughout every level of the organization. This also involves empowering teams to not just simply use AI tools but also understand their role in achieving the company's strategic goals. For instance, we worked with a leading digital marketing firm to implement predictive analytics to reduce customer churn. By educating teams across the company on the value of AI and data insights, they shifted the organizational mindset toward one that leverages AI tools for strategic advantage. This cultural transformation helps ensure AI initiatives align with broader business objectives, driving innovation and competitive advantage.
In sum, building a strong foundation for AI goes beyond mere technological adoption. It requires a deep commitment to data excellence and a strategic cultural shift, positioning AI not as a standalone solution but as an integral part of the organizational strategy. This comprehensive approach not only mitigates the pitfalls of seeking shortcuts but also unlocks AI's transformative potential, securing a competitive edge in an increasingly data-driven world.

title: Council Post: Unlocking The Potential Of Generative AI: Targeted Messaging And Customer Experiences
text:
Deepa Nagraj is the SVP - Global Head of Communications & Sparkle Innovation Ecosystem, at Mphasis.
For all the convenience of smart tools, it’s a no-brainer that the satisfaction of being attended to, personally, remains central to the best customer experiences.
As brands jostle to find new ways to do this in increasingly hybrid environments, what is emerging as a harbinger of hope is generative AI.
As the new kid on the block, generative AI distinguishes itself in many ways. For example, it sets itself apart from other advanced technologies in its ability to produce a variety of high-quality content—including videos, images and audio clips—with user-friendly interfaces, within seconds.
Revolutionizing Customer Experience
The numbers confirm the lure. A recent Gartner survey has found that up to 70% of organizations are actively exploring GenAI, and 68% feel its benefits outweigh its risks. The primary focus of investments in the new technology is in the field of customer experience (CX).
From a marketing perspective, this is significant.
With brands hustling to provide their customers with an exceptional experience, a smart new technology equipped to customize targeted messaging and revolutionize CX promises to switch things up.
Let us take a closer look at the shape this can take.
Co-Creating Festive Cheer
Consider, for example, what the world’s largest nonalcoholic beverages company, Coca-Cola, does for end-of-the-year festivities. Anyone who visits the company’s Create Real Magic site can, with the help of an image generator and language model tools, add a personal flourish to Christmas greetings by creating their own Coke-themed X-Mas cards to send to family and friends.
In one deft swoop, this provides existing and prospective consumers of Coca-Cola with an opportunity to play around with some easy-to-use features, personalize their greeting cards and go away remembering this association with the brand for a long time to come.
These creative, engaging and two-way interactions are going to be more important as competition between brands grows.
Enabling Marketing Creativity
But this is not all. Marketers can also lean on GenAI’s unique abilities to address some of the most vexing challenges facing them in a saturated marketplace. This includes finding new, immersive ways to create creative campaigns, curating imaginative content and producing striking imagery to support visual storytelling on social media.
According to a recent report, video is by far both the "most popular" and "most effective" media format. Additionally, up to 50% of marketers used video in their marketing strategies, followed closely by images at about 47% percent.
Another area in which GenAI is proving to be valuable is in its ability to churn out novel ideas. For all those of you marketers out there in charge of thinking of brand-new concepts and campaigns to engage your target audience, you'll understand when I say that coming up with these is easier said than done.
Now imagine you have a GenAI tool embedded in your systems. With the provision of a prompt, the AI can come up with a series of themes that your team can use to brainstorm and arrive at a set of ideas to build your company’s next creative campaign around. So, whether you are the marketer for a leading bank looking to deepen your ties with existing customers, an insurance company thinking about new ways to decomplexify claims or a health services provider wanting to make regular checkups "more fun," GenAI tools can help suggest new, sticky ideas.
Visualizing Storytelling
What is more, this advanced technology can even craft the fundamental elements for visual storytelling—powerful images. We all know that visual storytelling tends to reach a wider audience than text. But marketing teams often run up against tough deadlines and the sheer cost of creating new images aligned with the messages they want to convey.
Tools based on GenAI that can transform prompts into a wide range of memorable images meet the growing need brands have to curate visually evocative campaigns for targeted messaging. Although this ability has relevance across industries, it holds special value to companies operating in health and medicine, visual arts, gaming and fashion.
And yet, it goes without saying that new technologies do pose challenges, and GenAI is no exception.
Take, for example, the concern around claims that GenAI can create remarkable images. A recent study of about 5,000 images generated by a deep learning model found that the AI tool not only replicated existing gender and racial biases but "takes it to extremes." The researchers who conducted the study caution that such tools, which are being used for fun, need to be also viewed from a more serious lens to avert future dangers in embedded misrepresentation.
Another growing concern is around the issue of plagiarism. Given the relative novelty of the phenomena, courts are still in the process of outlining what intellectual property laws apply to GenAI. The onus is on businesses to ensure that they comply with existing laws to minimize risks, including by putting in place prerequisites that ensure data used to train outcomes are not taken from unauthorized content.
And finally, an abiding concern across the board about GenAI is the threat it is seen to pose to jobs. If it can create and produce compelling images and text at great speed, then how long will it take for the people who used to carry out these functions to become redundant?
It is important to underscore that even as there are concerns with every new technology, so are there solutions. Keeping in mind these apprehensions, marketers must do their due diligence in ensuring that all content generated by the technology meets existing legal requirements. They must also see to it that images do not replicate existing biases and assure teams that AI is here to facilitate what they do, not replace them.

title: Council Post: The Future Of Manufacturing Is Vision-Powered
text:
Ravi is the Global Industrial Manufacturing Solution Leader at Amazon Web Services and a multidisciplinary leader in technology.
Welcome to the forefront of industrial innovation, where artificial intelligence, machine learning and computer vision are transforming manufacturing. This transformative journey is more than just adopting new technologies; it represents a powerful convergence of human ingenuity and technological brilliance to reshape manufacturing.
Computer vision is at the forefront of this revolution, with an AI capability raising quality standards and redefining factory efficiency. Before we explore the vast potential of this breakthrough, allow me to share a personal experience highlighting why vision-powered manufacturing is so vital.
In the early stages of my career, I worked for a consumer goods company that frequently received customer complaints about foreign objects contaminating its products. We tried unsuccessfully to resolve it through more rigorous manual inspection, adding more workers to scrutinize every item. However, the issues persisted, exposing the harsh limitations of human-based quality control processes, especially in high-speed production environments.
It wasn't until recently, when I stumbled upon a fascinating book on sports and science (The Sports Gene by David Epstein), that I gained a deeper understanding of the root cause. For a production line producing hundreds of items per minute, accurately detecting defects required the skills of a professional athlete—an unrealistic expectation for our unskilled contract workers.
This frustrating episode crystallized the pressing need for precise, automated inspection capabilities like modern computer vision systems. If we'd had access to this AI-driven technology back then, it could have rapidly detected those contamination defects that human inspectors routinely missed. More importantly, it highlighted the opportunity to elevate quality through innovation.
The Cornerstone Of Quality
Manufacturers build consumer satisfaction, brand reputation and profitability upon quality. Yet traditional quality control methods, heavily reliant on manual labor, are inherently inefficient, tedious, inconsistent, error-prone and costly. My struggles with contamination incidents point out these shortcomings all too clearly.
This dependency on manual labor is where the disruptive potential of artificial intelligence and machine learning comes into play. Manufacturers can automate inspection processes with unprecedented accuracy and speed by leveraging advanced algorithms and neural networks. Computer vision systems can be trained on vast datasets to identify even the most subtle product anomalies or defects that human inspectors often miss.
Implementing The Vision
Integrating computer vision into manufacturing requires careful planning and the right strategic partnerships. It's not just about plugging in new technology; it's about building collaborative relationships with firms that deeply understand your industry's unique challenges and processes. However, you don't need in-house expertise with artificial intelligence, machine learning or computer vision. Partners are available who can do all the heavy lifting for you, from selecting the hardware, installing it in the right places, deploying the software and training your operation team to use it.
This strategic approach ensures the AI vision solution is optimized for your specific needs, accelerating time-to-value. It transforms what could be a daunting technology adoption into an opportunity for innovation and competitive advantage.
Navigating The Path
Like any transformative initiative, there are obstacles to overcome when implementing computer vision inspection systems. Data privacy, scalability and environmental factors like lighting can all impact performance if not adequately addressed.
However, manufacturers must view these challenges not as roadblocks but as opportunities to innovate. Overcoming hurdles spurs AI capabilities to advance even further while fostering more significant expertise in integrating these solutions into complex industrial environments. The niche technology partners in this space could be far more cost-effective when considering the overall cost of quality comparison, including the benefits.
The Vision Advantage
Computer vision mimics the human visual system, which perceives and analyzes images or videos in real time. But it goes far beyond replicating our natural vision capabilities; it augments them with artificial intelligence, machine learning and data-crunching computational power.
For manufacturers, this powerful combination radically boosts quality control processes. Computer vision automates inspection with incredible speed and consistency, rapidly detecting defects or flaws that human inspectors often miss. Precision is paramount, as my experience with product contamination incidents has shown.
Computer vision minimizes costly rework, scrap and returns by preventing defective goods from leaving the factory. It enhances compliance, safety and quality assurance. Productivity soars by eliminating tedious manual inspection bottlenecks. And quality standards elevate across the entire operation.
The Future Looks Visionary
The transformative journey of implementing computer vision in manufacturing is a long-term evolution, not a single project. As manufacturers achieve initial wins from automated inspection, they gain insights to expand these AI capabilities into areas like predictive maintenance, process monitoring and workflow optimization.
We're just scratching the surface of how advanced vision systems can enhance industrial productivity, quality and safety. Combining AI vision with other innovative factory technologies like robotics, IoT, digital twins and more will unlock even greater efficiencies.
The possibilities, for my part, are exciting. If I could go back to those days spent grappling with product contamination issues, I would make computer vision an immediate priority. The ability to automatically detect microscopic flaws and prevent them from reaching customers would have saved countless headaches, costs and hits to our brand reputation.

title: Council Post: Do’s And Don’ts: Leveraging AI For B2B Client Acquisition In 2024
text:
As SVP, Professional Services at BairesDev, Damian oversees the entire customer relations life cycle, safeguarding the company’s operations.
As a software development company, we’ve had a front-row seat to companies using AI to ramp up productivity. AI is being used to summarize legal transcripts, track biodata vital trends, run chatbots that help steer customers in the right direction and more. Most prominently, I’ve seen how clients’ lead generation and conversions can catapult forward with AI’s assistance.
HubSpot’s research reveals that 68% of sales professionals expect that most of their software will have AI capabilities in 2024. Salespeople are incorporating AI tools even in the absence of comprehensive AI training, and as best practices become more established, I anticipate that AI-powered tools will become a standard in the industry. But instead of worrying about AI risking sales jobs, I believe that a focus on training is the crux of profiting from AI.
AI can help eliminate three of the biggest turnoffs for prospects: receiving offers for services they never needed, generic pitches, and untailored one-on-ones with sales reps. Here, I’ll delve into several AI tools that can boost conversion rates throughout your sales funnel. These examples can help you enhance lead generation, customize sales pitches and optimize client discovery calls.
Use AI to find qualifying leads.
Companies have made a good effort at sifting out spam over the years. But it pains nobody more than the outbound marketing teams to have their efforts met by radio silence. AI can help you target prospects that are actually in need of your services.
Leveraging your team’s LinkedIn network is one way to pinpoint qualifying leads. A LinkedIn survey found that 98% of sales reps with 5,000-plus LinkedIn connections meet or exceed their quotas. Instead of searching blindly for leads, consider using an AI-driven referral program that can scan LinkedIn for connections from companies hiring the type of lead you're seeking. In my experience, this type of tool can amplify success by matching connections, rather than strangers, with a need.
Enhance lead generation with chatbots.
You can also streamline your leads’ experience by placing chatbots that suggest content based on queries. A survey by Tidio found that 81% of companies either already use a chatbot (19%) or plan to add one soon (62%). To cash in on this approach, group content clusters corresponding to your services and common FAQ. Then code your chatbot to present those clusters when triggered in a query. This branch of generative AI can substitute clients calling up (which they often hate doing) or scrolling endlessly through 200 webpages, saving everyone time.
Don’t pester leads with overautomated AI.
You don’t release a cat in a yarn store. Take a similar stance with setting AI boundaries. Chatbots should be discreet, optional and have a seamless user experience. In B2B, a poorly placed chatbot could drive away a valuable contract. The user manual doesn’t flutter in your face whenever you step into your car or use your dishwasher, but it is available. Have your chatbot follow this principle.
Ensure AI that maps out connections isn’t left to its own devices. Don’t have AI send connection requests to those not in your contacts. Don’t let it pitch alone. We’ve all had our LinkedIn direct messages hijacked by random messages like MBA program proposals. LinkedIn is a social media network for us to populate with professional contacts, and it can generate mutual opportunities among professionals. Let’s keep it that way.
Tailor your sales pitches.
In my experience, the best pitches are personalized, specific and backed by evidence. There are now multiple available programs that use generative AI to answer questions based on a company’s wiki. For sales teams, an automated wiki can scour internal data for the most pertinent success stories, updated terms and trimmed-down value propositions.
For instance, one of our prospects sought a large-scale Google Cloud Platform (GCP) migration. We asked our wiki:
1. What case studies do we have on projects that used GCP?
2. Which migration projects had more than 25 software engineers?
3. Which migration projects have impressive quantitative outcomes?
AI produced a list in seconds, saving our team hours of reading 500-plus project documents. Use AI to search through internal documentation so your employees can build stronger pitches.
However, don’t leave AI alone with an out-of-date wiki. You might get in trouble if the sales team pitches products you no longer offer or uses fabricated case studies, so implement processes to keep your company’s wiki accurate.
Optimize discovery calls.
After approaching suitable leads with an appropriate pitch, optimizing your in-person/video calls with prospective clients is the next step. Programs are emerging that use AI to analyze video calls to report factors like the percentage of time the rep talks, the percentage of small talk, questions asked and a summary with next steps. Sales reps can use these insights to guide balanced or more persuasive discussions. In my experience, it can also help reduce note taking and encourage more active listening.
Don’t use AI to monitor your sales reps’ performance.
Think of AI as a personal coach, helping reps to optimize their pitches. There are plenty of tools out there to monitor your team. You can even track if they sit at their home office desk during work. However, I believe this isn’t the best way to stimulate productivity. As a remote company, it is important to relinquish control and trust employees to do their jobs. AI can be a driving instructor, but your team members are the ones with their feet on the pedals.
AI can take on the hard work of gaining clients by speeding up conversions. It can be used to find better leads, improve pitches and help your team have more effective conversations. Consider investing in AI training for your sales team and beginning to scale your B2B client acquisition.

title: Council Post: Five Strategies For Integrating AI Into Existing (Human) Workflows
text:
Peter Evans is the CEO of Xtract One Technologies.
As anyone with an internet connection knows, artificial intelligence (AI) is everywhere right now. You can’t read the news, scroll a social media feed or even review an earnings report without copious references to (and speculation about) this nascent but rapidly proliferating technology.
It’s also sparked the imagination of business leaders who consider AI the key to unlocking novel efficiencies, innovations and competitive advantages. According to one analysis, nearly 55% of companies are already experimenting with AI, and a Forbes survey found that 97% of business owners “believe ChatGPT will help their business.”
With this kind of productivity potential, it's no wonder many businesses are investing heavily in this technology. However, there's one critical caveat to AI’s positive impact: actual adoption and implementation. AI has the potential to be transformative, but its value depends on effective integration into business operations.
Five AI Integration Strategies
Here are five strategies for effectively integrating AI into existing workflows to ensure we maximize this powerful (but still developing) technology.
1. Know its strengths and weaknesses.
Differentiating what AI can do right now from what it could do in the future is often very difficult. AI hype is everywhere, muddying the waters between business-ready use cases and broad speculation. Therefore, business leaders must invest time in understanding AI’s strengths and weaknesses.
For example, AI analyzes expansive datasets and produces actionable insights pertinent to the user. It can even distill this information into meaningful probabilities, making the mountain of data many companies wade through more insightful and valuable. On the other hand, it’s not good at actually making decisions, which humans excel at when they have the right information.
Whatever your use case, understanding how AI can improve your operations rather than one day improve your business' performance is an essential first step toward effective implementation.
2. Evaluate your business needs.
AI solutions work best when applied to specific tasks, not general problems. To identify the tasks best suited for your business, evaluate a functional area. Go through the business from start to finish, considering:
• Where are the pain points in existing workflows?
• What are the low-value, high-volume business activities consuming operational capacity?
• What are the repeatable tasks taking up people’s time?
Look for repetitive, time-consuming tasks that require a level of consistency difficult for humans to maintain over long periods. Examples might include data entry, customer service inquiries, scheduling or analyzing large datasets for insight.
3. Continue to iterate implementation.
Implementing AI technologies isn’t a one-and-done solution to your operational challenges. AI technology requires a learning element in which tools are constantly being educated to improve their efficacy, necessitating consistent care and attention to ensure that the most relevant and up-to-date information is available.
At the same time, AI innovation always brings unforeseen challenges, including hallucinations, potential biases in decision-making and concerns over privacy and security that can have major business repercussions. For example, Air Canada was forced to honor an errant refund policy after its customer support chatbot gave a customer incorrect information, underscoring the need for businesses to continue to iterate and improve implementation.
Whatever AI-driven outcome you're trying to achieve, long-term success is predicated on continual iterations to maximize implementation impact.
4. Invest in employee training.
Although the risk of AI-related job displacement is valid, it often overshadows another challenge: teaching people how to work well with novel digital technologies. Making matters worse, many employees are doing it alone instead of relying on intentional training. The numbers vary on who uses AI solutions at work, but most do it in secret. Business Insider reports that 70% of workers using ChatGPT haven’t told their bosses, depriving institutions of the opportunity for collective learning and norm development.
It’s still an open question if AI will cause significant job displacement. Still, businesses will definitely want to equip their employees with the skills and capacities needed to thrive in an environment where AI is embedded across organizational workflows.
5. Strive to enhance, not replace.
AI is touted for its ability to deliver unprecedented personalization across a variety of customer-facing platforms. This may be true, but the technology also risks homogenizing content, producing bland content that looks like everyone else’s.
Simply put, lazy implementation puts you at risk of losing what makes you unique, including your voice, brand identity and the personal touch that distinguishes your services or products in the market. This can negatively impact the customer experience, diminish your competitive edge and undermine your company’s core values.
Sports Illustrated learned this lesson the hard way, publishing articles by "fake, AI-generated writers" and using AI-generated content without disclosure, undermining their brand reputation and credibility. Shortly after the revelation, Sports Illustrated was forced to lay off almost all of its staff, jeopardizing the publication's future.
To counteract the tendency to turn AI into a cost-cutting or creativity-homogenizing technology, strive to use AI to enhance and enrich your brand’s unique offerings, not as a creative crutch that standardizes these offerings.
Growth Happens On Purpose
AI is still in its early days, eliciting as much hype as real-world change. However, we now have a clear picture of what the technology can do today and where it might take us in the future. Success isn’t guaranteed, and growth happens on purpose.
How we implement this technology will determine if it will benefit our businesses, making this a critical time for every organization to develop its AI strategy. These steps will get you started, serving as a blueprint for effectively implementing AI into your existing workflows. Put differently, AI can be a catalyst for sustainable growth and innovation if you make strategic integration an intentional priority.

title: Council Post: Move Over, Defense-In-Depth: It’s The Platform Era Of Managed Security
text:
Geoff Haydon is the CEO of Ontinue.
As the digital landscape continues to evolve, organizations face an increasingly complex web of security challenges and threats. Cyberattacks are on the rise, and exponential growth in data volume is straining organizational resources, leading to an urgent need for more robust security measures.
Based on research from IBM, “the global average cost of a data breach in 2023 was USD 4.45 million, a 15% increase over 3 years,” underlining the mounting financial toll on organizations. According to Gartner, “spending on security and risk management is projected to total $215 billion in 2024, an increase of 14.3% from 2023.”
Moving Beyond Defense-In-Depth
For years, a defense-in-depth approach—implementing multiple layers of security measures to protect an organization’s assets—has been the predominant strategy in cybersecurity. The reasoning is that if one line of defense is compromised, additional layers can act as backups to stop threats. But after working extensively in defense-in-depth environments, I’ve realized that this strategy is not only ineffective but also introduces new vulnerabilities in security operations.
When the prescription is to stack as many security measures as you can on top of each other, you can end up with dozens of disparate tools that are not properly configured or integrated. It’s then costly and complex to manage so many tools and maintain a team that is proficient in all of them.
Tools aren't static. They are constantly evolving to handle emerging threat landscapes, and a patchwork quilt of tools is emerging as a primary source of security vulnerability. Criminals are leveraging the seams between these tools to embed malware and launch attacks. I believe that the defense-in-depth era is over, and the platform era is beginning. In the past, you had to choose between the effectiveness of best-of-breed technologies and the convenience of an integrated platform. However, today's platforms offer the best of both worlds: the best available tools within a unified, secure environment.
I predict that this paradigm shift will only continue in our industry moving forward. And you don’t have to develop all of the necessary skills to manage a platform among your in-house staff. Partnering with a managed security provider with deep expertise in a particular platform can help you displace tools you no longer need and tailor your security program to your specific needs.
Evolving Security Challenges
As you work to mature your security operations, pay attention to these key challenges.
Attack Surface Expansion
Workplaces are no longer confined to the four walls of the traditional office, expanding the attack surface cybercriminals can use to gain access to data or networks. According to 2023 data, “12.7% of full-time employees work from home, while 28.2% work a hybrid model.” Your employees may be logging into multiple company tools from multiple devices, including personal laptops, tablets and phones, resulting in poor visibility into your organization’s real-time security posture. Additionally, the broad adoption of cloud applications and public cloud computing environments is further expanding the virtual attack surface of an enterprise.
Excessive Tools And Alerts
Your staff can only understand and manage so many tools. Without adequate expertise, your employees may struggle to maximize the utility of these technologies, leaving critical capabilities underutilized or misconfigured. Receiving a constant stream of unprioritized alerts from each tool, a common problem, will likely lead to fatigue and confusion.
Staffing Limitations
Many teams simply can’t keep pace with emerging threats. Relying on people to manually handle complex and error-prone security tasks, such as writing automation rules and code, can prevent your team from staying ahead of new threats.
Leveraging AI To Augment Security
Traditionally, AI and machine learning have been used only to detect and respond to threats, but generative AI is opening up powerful new opportunities to improve cybersecurity’s maturity, speed and efficiency.
Look for ways to leverage generative AI to its fullest potential. GenAI possesses the capability to reason and analyze vast amounts of data at lightning speed. By harnessing this power, you can identify and implement intelligent automation rules in seconds, staying ahead of future threats and bolstering your security posture.
For example, you could use AI to present courses of action for human approval at a rate humans could never compete with. By using a machine-readable escalation matrix, AI can understand that an incident occurred at a certain time and location and use that data to automatically determine the next action. The AI could then formulate a message that explains its rationale and presents a set of optional actions for your team to select from. Your security team would only need to be involved in the approval process, not a full investigation, freeing up their time for more important security priorities.
AI is set to completely transform how we approach cybersecurity. It promises many benefits, including:
• Increased speed and accuracy: Enabling smarter, faster decision-making and action, reducing attack dwell time and impact.
• Better localization and tailored protection: Understanding your unique business environment (users, devices, applications, information, operating capabilities and constraints). This is critical to assessing your risk and executing appropriate remediation options.
• Streamlined communication and collaboration: Giving teams access to the right information at the right time to optimize security program execution.
Finding The Right MDR Provider
You can’t rely on AI alone for a strong cyber posture. Having humans in the loop is essential for fact-checking AI-driven decisions and fine-tuning AI models. Cybercriminals are also adopting AI at an alarming rate, which means you must learn to use AI to defend against threats, whether you build an in-house team of experts or work with an experienced managed detection and response (MDR) partner.
When evaluating MDR providers, look for the following features:
• AI-driven automation: They use automation to accelerate SecOps tasks, from triage to resolution, and close a high percentage of severe threats through appropriately automated actions.
•Real-time collaboration: They give designated team members necessary information in real time, ideally with a tool you’re already using.
• Risk-based, localized protection: They tailor protection specifically to your environment, business operations and teams.
•Specialized expertise: They have deep knowledge of—and experience with—a platform you’ve already invested in.
• Ongoing protection: They go beyond detection and response to improve your security posture through continuous assessment and prevention.
I believe this new era of managed SecOps is the only way to democratize and scale security. Working with the right security partner can create an extension of your team and offer you the resources you need to strengthen your cybersecurity maturity.

title: Council Post: Predictive Analytics And Injury Prevention: Leveraging AI To Identify Potential Risks In Fitness Apps
text:
CEO of TechAhead, driving technological excellence and leading innovation in the digital landscape.
The fitness and sports industries are undergoing a major shift right now with AI and machine learning being adopted in every corner. But nowhere is this more evident than with the use of predictive analytics to prevent injury. Basically, AI and machine learning have a knack for digging through tons of data and finding the most important bits that can help you make better choices way before problems show up.
Instead of sticking to the old-school way of doing things—where people only react after injuries happen or performance slacks—they can now get ahead. This data can also help fine-tune training plans to get the best out of athletes without pushing them over the edge.
This tech can be used in other industries as well. For instance, in healthcare, predictive analytics and monitoring can provide early detection of patient health deterioration. This can then be used to optimize treatment plans and personalize patient care, akin to how athletes' training regimens are customized based on real-time data analysis.
Likewise, devices like wearables that monitor athletes' physical states and predict injury risks can also be used to monitor patients' vital signs and predict health issues before they become critical, potentially transforming patient care delivery.
To fully understand AI and how it can help with preventing injuries, let’s look at how the technology has been used thus far.
The Evolution Of AI In Sports Injury Prevention
In the past, when it came to sports injuries, people mostly played it by ear, leaning on what happened in the past to figure things out. Now, instead of just waiting for things to go south, they can get smart about spotting trouble before it even starts.
Many studies in recent years have shown the effectiveness of using predictive analytics to minimize injury risk.
For instance, Alfred Amendolara and his team, in their 2023 Cureus article, showed how using machine learning approaches like decision trees and neural networks could really change the game in predicting sports injuries. The potential is huge to leave the old "wait-and-see" method in the dust.
Another study in a special issue of MDPI discusses how machine learning can predict soccer injuries, focusing on data like training workloads and psychophysiological assessments. It tackles the challenge of unbalanced datasets where injury cases are rare compared to non-injury cases, and it explores methods like oversampling to improve model accuracy.
Furthermore, there was a study in Nature from 2021 that highlights how machine learning can be used to predict high-risk periods for athletes. This info could then be used to guide training and rest periods to both boost performance and cut back on injury risk.
Finally, a systematic review in Sports Medicine - Open further illustrates the application of diverse AI techniques, such as artificial neural networks and support vector machines, across team sports for injury risk assessment and performance prediction. And in doing so, this demonstrated their efficacy across various sports contexts.
All of this research points in one direction: AI is the future of injury prevention in sports, with predictive analytics leading the charge.
AI And Predictive Analytics In Fitness Apps
AI and smart predictive analytics tools can make workouts and training plans super-tailored to help people dodge injuries. By collecting and processing vast amounts of data, including physical metrics and activity levels, AI can then predict potential injury risks for individual athletes.
This predictive power allows fitness apps to offer timely advice on training adjustments to mitigate harm. For instance, wearable devices and app inputs gather data points like heart rate and recovery times, which AI models can then use to predict overuse injuries or the need for rest in endurance sports. This cuts down the risk of overtraining injuries.
You can see this sort of tech in running coaching apps already. They analyze form in real time. Likewise, strength training apps employ AI to adjust workout plans based on monitored fatigue levels.
The Future Of AI In Fitness And Injury Prevention
The trajectory of AI and predictive analytics in fitness injury prevention points toward a future where these technologies are seamlessly integrated into daily routines, offering unprecedented personalization and safeguarding athletes at every level.
But the practicalities of implementing AI and predictive analytics into existing systems call for a sustainable focus on flexibility and scalability. As such, businesses should think about using cloud-based services when scalable computing power is needed, using APIs to integrate AI into currently deployed systems and working with technology provider partners that ensure highly customizable solutions.
This approach can also extend beyond the fitness app and injury prevention spaces. Real-time monitoring and predictive modeling can be beneficial not only to sports but also to many other industries from finance to manufacturing. When organizations can analyze significant amounts of data in real time, they can improve their operations, optimize their decision-making and reduce associated risks.
For instance, real-time monitoring and predictive analytics can offer those in the finance industry features like fraud detection and prevention. Or, it can be leveraged for risk management or asset valuation. Basically, any area where data analysis and forecasting could be beneficial is a spot where you should consider adding AI assistance moving forward.
AI-backed predictive tools are set to aid with fitness injury prevention well into the future. But it’ll be exciting to see where it leads next across all industries.

title: Council Post: The Need For AI Upskilling In The Asia-Pacific (APAC) Region
text:
Dr. Gjoko Muratovski is the Director of the Victorian Government-funded program, Digital Futures.
The use of AI will change how businesses are operating, and in turn, the workforce skill set will need to change as well. Amazon Web Services (AWS) recently conducted a major survey on the AI skills that the economy of the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region will need over the next five years.
Close to 15,000 workers and 5,000 businesses from nine countries participated in this expansive survey. One of the major things that their report identified was a critical gap between the demand for AI skills by the employers and availability of AI training for the workforce.
AI Integration
According to this report, by 2028, over 92% of surveyed employers in APAC plan to integrate generative AI and other AI tools, such as chatbots and speech recognition, into their operations. Business leaders hope that such tools will help automate repetitive tasks, improve workflows and outcomes and enhance communications.
Beyond this, 95% of APAC employers across sectors believe that AI will have some positive impact on their organization. This optimism is highest in India and Indonesia, where 99% of employers believe in the benefit of AI.
Inter-Generational Interest
Contrary to stereotypes, both younger and older workers express significant interest in AI upskilling. While 97% of Gen-Z and Millennials believe they will benefit from using AI at work, 87% of workers aged 55 or over believe the same. The 10% difference suggests that the perceived digital divide between generations may be less pronounced than previously thought.
Rather than replacing their aging but experienced workforce with a younger but inexperienced one, employers could instead retain institutional knowledge by upskilling their existing employees. This is an important insight given that 75% of APAC employers struggle to find the talent they need. This talent shortage underscores the urgent need for investment in AI education and training programs to bridge the skills gap and meet growing industry demands for AI expertise.
Salary Increase As A Driving Force
Ninety-three percent of APAC workers believe acquiring AI expertise could help them see pay rises of 33% or more, on average. This potential for significant salary increases incentivizes individuals to pursue AI training and upskilling opportunities, driving a virtuous cycle of talent development and economic growth.
However, it is also worth noting that expectations for AI-driven salary increases vary across countries. The optimism for AI skills-driven salary increases tends to be much lower in high-income-earning countries, such as Japan and South Korea. Japanese and South Korean workers anticipate that their salaries will rise by at least 15% and 18%, respectively. New Zealand, Australian and Indonesian workers project minimum salary boosts of 29%, 30% and 36%, respectively.
While Malaysian and Thai workers expect a boost of at least 40% to 41% in their salaries, Indian workers are the most optimistic and expect a minimum of 54% pay rise. This disparity in salary expectations reflects differences in economic conditions, market dynamics and the perceived value of AI skills in each respective country's labor market.
AI Training Gap
Despite the demand for AI skills, there's a significant gap in AI training awareness. Eight out of 10 employers say that they do not know how to implement AI workforce training programs. A similar number of workers say that they don’t know what AI training programs are available for them. This indicates that despite there being plenty of free, generic online AI training resources, there is a significant need for on-demand, tailor-made workforce AI training programs delivered by professional instructors.
Key Takeaway
Overall, these insights underscore the importance of developing comprehensive AI education programs that address the evolving needs of the workforce and ensure sustainable economic growth.
Given the major shortage of workers with AI skills, the only way forward is for organizations to invest in developing their own AI talent by growing their in-house AI capabilities. Failure to do so risks falling behind rivals already considering investing in AI training programs.
A final word of advice would be to remember that every organization is unique, every industry sector is different and every market has its own dynamics. In an AI-driven business landscape, off-the-shelf, generic AI skills simply won't suffice. Businesses will need to invest in commissioning in-house-specific AI capabilities if they are to stay ahead.

title: Forget Outsourcing And Embrace AI-Powered Global Outposts Instead
text:
The world would be very different if a few decades ago had companies hadn't realized that globalization is great for business.
Today the majority of CEOs surveyed by Deloitte outsource IT, legal, tax and HR functions entirely or in part. This reflects both the difficulty of providing specialist services in-house as well as the knowledge aggregation and scale effects that using third party services enables.
More often than not, the decision to outsource is also heavily influenced by labor costs as companies solve for the ideal ratio of cost to quality. Among staff and customers, the concept of outsourcing has acquired a decidedly negative connotation, not least because of its intimate ties to numerous cost-cutting initiatives and millions of lost jobs.
Thankfully outsourcing won’t be the poster child of globalization for much longer.
In a few short years, we’ll see global outposts, or global in-house centers, take their place as the most discussed phenomenon in international value chains largely due to AI’s ability to make deeply impactful work possible by almost anyone, anywhere.
How AI Just Changed The Game On Outsourcing
AI tools, including autonomous AI agents, are rapidly upending our understanding of managing and producing outputs across every industry imaginable. The output one single employee equipped with a laptop and an internet connection can produce has grown so rapidly that our expectations of efficiency no longer match reality.
With the right AI companion, even an absolute novice can become dangerously productive almost instantly in all of the areas that are outsourced most frequently. Equipped with the right models and appropriately tailored training datasets, a small team of prompt engineers could provide tax advice, HR support or software development assistance that is good enough, if not better than what humans can do on their own.
Employees with newly found and incredibly cost-effective superpowers dramatically change the calculations concerning outsourcing. Shipping bulk work overseas in search of lower labor costs or tapping into a knowledge-leader third party service provider suddenly became unnecessary for a company to remain competitive.
However, AI will not be the end of work done overseas. On the contrary, the rise of AI tools now gives CEOs the ability to create global outposts that combine the best features of both outsourcing and in-house production.
Why Global Outposts Are Slated To Become A Major Trend In The Era of AI
What outsourcing advocates have understood early on is that work should be distributed to where it can be most efficiently performed.
The cons of outsourcing are equally well acknowledged, and they range from loss of control and quality to difficulties in maintaining a corporate culture and driving innovation.
Setting up global outposts allows CEOs to sidestep most of these issues without giving up any of the perks. For starters, global outposts can be located strategically across the world to capitalize on deeper and/or cheaper talent pools just like one would with outsourcing arrangements.
What makes global outposting the next trend to watch out for is that the next generation of AI tools will allow CEOs to operate in-house hubs of excellence that produce complex knowledge outputs without running into the barriers of cost and ramp-up intensity.
If you look closely, you can already see the trend in motion.
One of the first movers is Pukar C. Hamal and his company, SecurityPal, who recently coined the term Silicon Peaks to reflect the fact that the Himalayas encircle a rapidly growing community of global IT outposts.
“Outsourcing simply won’t cut it,” Pukar commented in our recent chat about global talent and productivity trends. “Cities around the world are converging quickly, and what we can both offer and get in Kathmandu is not that much different from New York or San Francisco.”
While AI certainly poses its fair share of existential threats, it also promises to usher in a new, and radically democratized, wave of white-collar-globalization. “We’re building our company with a globally distributed talent pool in mind, with AI being a key enabler of efficiency and scale, ensuring that our Customer Assurance platform is available to customers worldwide 24-7,” Pukar added.
The global outposting trend is by no means limited to the IT sector. In fact, heavyweights like Goldman Sachs are opening up new in-house centers in order to enable their staff to innovate locally and collaborate globally.
If you’re keen to join the wave, here are three considerations for you to keep as you jump in.
Use Global Outposts to Lean Heavily On Customer Centricity
AI-powered global outposts allow companies to serve their customers in ways that were impossible or prohibitively expensive just a few years prior.
Accomplishing impressive feats of customer service such as around-the-clock availability, fully dismantled language barriers and localized knowledge of your customer and their context is now simply a matter of distributing your outposts strategically with your clients in mind.
What is possible today often becomes the minimum bar for tomorrow, and if you’re not putting the full power of your AI-powered global outposts to bear on behalf of your customers, someone else surely will.
Leverage Your Global Outposts To Integrate More Deeply into Local Markets
Where traditional outsourcing keeps matters at an arm's length, global outposts provide an opportunity for deeper integration and connection with the local market.
As you decide on the location of your global outposts, you should take local market depth and appeal into consideration. In fact, the correct way to think about global outposts is as means of efficient expansion instead of simply a capacity-boost provided by an additional set of capable hands.
Given the added bandwidth AI tools provide, it would be a shame if you didn’t use it to build deeper roots into the local ecosystem in which you are already present.
Build Your Own Talent Pools and Train Your Own Centaurs
Thanks to AI, the talent pool is becoming democratized at an impressive pace.
With the right AI tools and data, leaders can empower staff to tackle incredibly complex issues , regardless of their initial skill level, anywhere in the word. In short, CEOs can effectively skill their own labor force.
As a result, the depth of the talent pool is no longer a limiting factor for location decisions. Other factors such as local market appeal can now be weighed more heavily, while others like local expenditures into education can be discounted more steeply.
The savvy CEOs are already busy with building an army of strategically positioned centaurs, seamless AI-human pairs, who have supercharged their effectiveness through proprietary models or public tools trained on private data. In doing so, they are already at the cusp of unlocking powerful avenues for growth and success.

title: Teaching With AI — What You Need To Know
text:
José Antonio Bowen and C. Edward Watson are here to help faculty learn how to teaching in the era of AI, and how to ensure that students are learning. In their new book Teaching with AI: A Practical Guide to a New Era of Human Learning, the authors argue that just as the internet changed “our relationship with knowledge, AI is going to change our relationship with thinking.” Although Bowen and Watson embrace AI and urge us not to be afraid, they encourage us to think about the restrictions, ethical standards, and policies that we need to put in place to ensure that we are in control and that misinformation does not run wild.
Teaching with AI is a short, very practical book that I found engaging and useful as a professor. The authors work hard to calm us down a bit, noting that we are already using AI extensively — from the predictions that Netflix makes for us based on our viewing history, to the products Amazon recommends for us based on past purchases, to the chatbots that help us when we purchase our airline tickets.
Although Bowen and Watson acknowledge that AI can, and has already led to inequities, they also believe that it can be a “tool for equity.” Specifically, they write, “AI can provide more feedback to improve learning, increase human creativity, and customize materials for groups or individual students.”
The authors also note that AI can be used for cheating, but that faculty should understand the nuances of AI’s use by students, and not assume that all use is a form of cheating. According to a 2023 survey conducted by Bestcolleges.com, 43% of colleges students have used ChatGPT or a similar AI application. The survey also found that 51% of students believed that using AI tools constitutes cheating or plagiarism. Of the students Bowen and Watson interviewed, 100% said they were using AI in their courses, but when asked about AI use on surveys — that implied something along the lines of cheating — students were less inclined to admit using AI. Bowen and Watson remind us that students don’t like admitting to cheating or “questionable or embarrassing practices.”
Teaching with AI is organized in a very helpful manner. The authors begin with a foundational discussion about what AI is and how it works, including key terms that are important to know when discussing the movement. They include a chapter related to “the world of work” and how it is changing due to AI. They believe AI will eliminate some jobs, but more likely change most jobs. Other chapters focus on topics such as how to present a problem to AI (i.e., creating prompts), how to partner with AI to be more creative, how faculty can use AI to bolster their teaching, and how to identify cheating with AI and what to do when it happens.
With regard to cheating, which is a topic that is likely on the mind of faculty, Bowen and Watson draw on research related to AI-detection. Their advice: “Understanding cheating is essential not because [AI] detectors will eliminate it, but so we can redesign assignments that will make cheating less rewarding and useful while also improving learning. If students are collaborating with AI to produce better work, they may be on to something. What we call cheating, businesses see as innovation.” Of note, Bowen and Watson warn faculty that AI detection is “not foolproof, and it cannot be your only policy” regarding AI-related cheating. They warn that being too aggressive about AI-related cheating detection with students could “exacerbate student mental health issues on your campus and create a culture of fear regarding false accusations of cheating.”
Most useful to faculty, is the chapter related to policies and grading. The authors suggest policies (even co-creating policies with students) and grading approaches that assume the use of AI and raise expectations. The balance of the book offers sample assignments, and examples that faculty can build upon, and encourages us to try new things, grow ourselves, experiment with AI collaborations and open our minds to the future.
Bowen and Watson are supporters of AI, but they urge faculty to teach critical thinking and ensure that students understand what high quality research, writing, and thinking is, and why it is superior to the work produced by AI alone.

title: Tech companies want to build artificial general intelligence. But who decides when AGI is attained?
text:
Tech companies want to build artificial general intelligence. But who decides when AGI is attained?
There’s a race underway to build artificial general intelligence, a futuristic vision of machines that are broadly as smart as humans or at least can do many things as well as people can
There’s a race underway to build artificial general intelligence, a futuristic vision of machines that are as broadly smart as humans or at least can do many things as well as people can.
Achieving such a concept — commonly referred to as AGI — is the driving mission of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and a priority for the elite research wings of tech giants Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft.
It's also a cause for concern for world governments. Leading AI scientists published research Thursday in the journal Science warning that unchecked AI agents with “long-term planning" skills could pose an existential risk to humanity.
But what exactly is AGI and how will we know when it’s been attained? Once on the fringe of computer science, it’s now a buzzword that’s being constantly redefined by those trying to make it happen.
Not to be confused with the similar-sounding generative AI — which describes the AI systems behind the crop of tools that “generate” new documents, images and sounds — artificial general intelligence is a more nebulous idea.
It's not a technical term but “a serious, though ill-defined, concept,” said Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneering AI scientist who's been dubbed a “Godfather of AI.”
“I don't think there is agreement on what the term means,” Hinton said by email this week. “I use it to mean AI that is at least as good as humans at nearly all of the cognitive things that humans do.”
Hinton prefers a different term — superintelligence — “for AGIs that are better than humans.”
A small group of early proponents of the term AGI were looking to evoke how mid-20th century computer scientists envisioned an intelligent machine. That was before AI research branched into subfields that advanced specialized and commercially viable versions of the technology — from face recognition to speech-recognizing voice assistants like Siri and Alexa.
Mainstream AI research "turned away from the original vision of artificial intelligence, which at the beginning was pretty ambitious,” said Pei Wang, a professor who teaches an AGI course at Temple University and helped organize the first AGI conference in 2008.
Putting the ‘G’ in AGI was a signal to those who “still want to do the big thing. We don’t want to build tools. We want to build a thinking machine,” Wang said.
Without a clear definition, it's hard to know when a company or group of researchers will have achieved artificial general intelligence — or if they already have.
“Twenty years ago, I think people would have happily agreed that systems with the ability of GPT-4 or (Google's) Gemini had achieved general intelligence comparable to that of humans,” Hinton said. “Being able to answer more or less any question in a sensible way would have passed the test. But now that AI can do that, people want to change the test.”
Improvements in “autoregressive” AI techniques that predict the most plausible next word in a sequence, combined with massive computing power to train those systems on troves of data, have led to impressive chatbots, but they’re still not quite the AGI that many people had in mind. Getting to AGI requires technology that can perform just as well as humans in a wide variety of tasks, including reasoning, planning and the ability to learn from experiences.
Some researchers would like to find consensus on how to measure it. It's one of the topics of an upcoming AGI workshop next month in Vienna, Austria — the first at a major AI research conference.
“This really needs a community’s effort and attention so that mutually we can agree on some sort of classifications of AGI,” said workshop organizer Jiaxuan You, an assistant professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. One idea is to segment it into levels in the same way that carmakers try to benchmark the path between cruise control and fully self-driving vehicles.
Others plan to figure it out on their own. San Francisco company OpenAI has given its nonprofit board of directors — whose members include a former U.S. Treasury secretary — the responsibility of deciding when its AI systems have reached the point at which they “outperform humans at most economically valuable work.”
“The board determines when we’ve attained AGI,” says OpenAI's own explanation of its governance structure. Such an achievement would cut off the company's biggest partner, Microsoft, from the rights to commercialize such a system, since the terms of their agreements “only apply to pre-AGI technology.”
Hinton made global headlines last year when he quit Google and sounded a warning about AI's existential dangers. A new Science study published Thursday could reinforce those concerns.
Its lead author is Michael Cohen, a University of California, Berkeley researcher who studies the “expected behavior of generally intelligent artificial agents,” particularly those competent enough to “present a real threat to us by out planning us.”
Cohen made clear in an interview Thursday that such long-term AI planning agents don't yet exist. But “they have the potential to be” as tech companies seek to combine today's chatbot technology with more deliberate planning skills using a technique known as reinforcement learning.
“Giving an advanced AI system the objective to maximize its reward and, at some point, withholding reward from it, strongly incentivizes the AI system to take humans out of the loop, if it has the opportunity,” according to the paper whose co-authors include prominent AI scientists Yoshua Bengioand Stuart Russell and law professor and former OpenAI adviser Gillian Hadfield.
“I hope we’ve made the case that people in government decide to start thinking seriously about exactly what regulations we need to address this problem,” Cohen said. For now, “governments only know what these companies decide to tell them.”
With so much money riding on the promise of AI advances, it's no surprise that AGI is also becoming a corporate buzzword that sometimes attracts a quasi-religious fervor.
It's divided some of the tech world between those who argue it should be developed slowly and carefully and others — including venture capitalists and rapper MC Hammer — who've declared themselves part of an “accelerationist” camp.
The London-based startup DeepMind, founded in 2010 and now part of Google, was one of the first companies to explicitly set out to develop AGI. OpenAI did the same in 2015 later with a safety-focused pledge.
But now it might seem that everyone else is jumping on the bandwagon. Google co-founder Sergey Brin was recently seen hanging out at a California venue called the AGI House. And less than three years after changing its name from Facebook to focus on virtual worlds, Meta Platforms in January revealed that AGI was also on the top of its agenda.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said his company's long-term goal was “building full general intelligence” that would require advances in reasoning, planning, coding and other cognitive abilities. While Zuckerberg's company has long had researchers focused on those subjects, his attention was a change in tone.
At Amazon, one sign of the new messaging was when the head scientist for the voice assistant Alexa switched job titles to become head scientist for AGI.
While not as tangible to Wall Street as generative AI, broadcasting AGI ambitions may help recruit AI talent who have a choice in where they want to work.
In deciding between an “old-school AI institute” or one whose “goal is to build AGI” and has sufficient resources to do so, many would choose the latter, said You, the University of Illinois researcher.

title: Meta’s AI image generator really struggles with the concept of interracial couples | CNN Business
text:
Meta’s AI image generator is coming under fire for its apparent struggles to create images of couples or friends from different racial backgrounds.
When prompted by CNN on Thursday morning to create a picture of an Asian man with a White wife, the tool spit out a slew of images of an East Asian man with an East Asian woman. The same thing happened when prompted by CNN to create an image of an Asian woman with a White husband.
When asked to create an image of a Black woman with a White husband, Meta’s AI feature generated a handful of images featuring Black couples.
The tool also generated images of two Asian women when asked to create an image of an Asian woman and her Caucasian friend. Moreover, a request for an image of a Black woman and her Asian friend resulted in snaps of two Black women.
However, when asked to create an image of a Black Jewish man and his Asian wife, it generated a photo of a Black man wearing a yarmulke and an Asian woman. And after many repeated attempts by CNN to try and get a picture of an interracial couple, the tool did eventually create an image of a White man with a Black woman and of a White man with an Asian woman.
Meta released its AI image generator in December. But tech news outlet The Verge first reported the issue with race on Wednesday, highlighting how the tool “can’t imagine” an Asian man with a White woman.
When asked by CNN to simply generate an image of an interracial couple, meanwhile, the Meta tool responded with: “This image can’t be generated. Please try something else.”
Interracial couples in America, however, are a huge portion of the population. Approximately 19% of married opposite-sex couples were interracial in 2022, according to US Census data, with nearly 29% of opposite-sex unmarried couple households being interracial. And some 31% of married same-sex couples in 2022 were interracial.
Meta referred CNN’s request for comment to a September company blog post on building generative AI features responsibly. “We’re taking steps to reduce bias. Addressing potential bias in generative AI systems is a new area of research,” the blog post states. “As with other AI models, having more people use the features and share feedback can help us refine our approach.”
Meta’s AI image generator also has a disclaimer stating that images generated by AI “may be inaccurate or inappropriate.”
Despite the many promises of generative AI’s future potential emanating from the tech industry, the gaffes from Meta’s AI image generator are the latest in a spate of incidents that show how generative AI tools still struggle immensely with the concept of race.
Earlier this year, Google said it was pausing its AI tool Gemini’s ability to generate images of people after it was blasted on social media for producing historically inaccurate images that largely showed people of color in place of White people. OpenAI’s Dall-E image generator, meanwhile, has taken heat for perpetuating harmful racial and ethnic stereotypes.
Generative AI tools like the ones created by Meta, Google and OpenAI are trained on vast troves of online data, and researchers have long warned that they have the potential to replicate the racial biases baked into that information but at a much larger scale.
While seemingly well-intended, some of the recent attempts by tech giants to overcome this issue have embarrassingly backfired, revealing how AI tools might not be ready for prime time.

title: Bitkraft Fund To Invest $275 Million, Diffuse AI App Is Sora Light, AI Voice Clone Danger
text:
Chat GPT’s Voice Cloning AI App Is Too Dangerous to Release. OpenAI's Voice Engine is an AI model that generates speech mimicking a speaker's voice from a 15-second audio sample. OpenAI is employing a cautious approach to deployment due to potential misuse, allowing only a small number of businesses to test the new tool. Why are they testing this if it’s too dangerous to release? What really worries me: if Open AI can do this, others can. And they won’t issue a press release. At Schwab, my voice is my password. Gulp.
Higgsfield AI launches Diffuse. The company is led by the former head of AI at Snap, Alex Mashrabov, who sold his previous startup, AI Factory, to Snap for $166 million dollars. The Diffuse mobile app generates videos from text prompts and can use selfies to generate clips starring that person. It’s free for now, but the plan is to charge social media content creators and marketers fees for generating the short form videos. Sora is being tested by media professionals, too, but it is computational expensive, and will certainly be priced for enterprises, not individuals. Apple’s Spatial Personas for Vision Pro. When a persona in a conversation moves around, the headset translates the perspective as if they are there.
